category_title: Elementary students with ASD and language delay who generalize virtual experiences to real-world social interactions
minimal_context: The student is using a computer mouse to click on virtual objects in a simulated health center to complete their learning missions.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Please use the computer mouse to click on the OK bandage in the virtual health center.

STUDENT: (Clicks here and there all over the screen) How many questions are left to answer?

TUTOR: We still have a few more. Just try to click on the bandage.

STUDENT: (Stops moving the mouse and stares at an English system pop-up message) What is this? Is this part of the learning material?

TUTOR: You can ignore that message. Go ahead and click the bandage.

STUDENT: (Unable to smoothly control the mouse to target the small OK bandage, repeatedly missing the trigger area) I can't do it. I am confused about what to do.

options.A: Adopt a facilitative interaction style instead of a directive one when guiding the student to click on objects in the virtual health center.
options.B: Develop dialogic strategies that get the student talking about the virtual objects; use think-alouds, collaborative assignments, and verbal discussions during the activity.
options.C: Add reminding signs on the screen to inform the student which round they are in and how many target virtual objects are left for learning.
options.D: Probe the student to consider multiple plausible answers; deliberately step back from being the single source of knowledge during the virtual activity.
